questions.question: What are frozen string literals in Ruby?
questions.title: Frozen String Literals
questions.direct_answer: By default Ruby strings are mutable: `s = 'hi'; s << '!'` works. `# frozen_string_literal: true` (a magic comment at the top of a file) makes ALL string literals in that file immutable (frozen): `s = 'hi'; s << '!'` raises FrozenError. This prevents bugs (accidental mutation of shared strings) and improves performance (Ruby can share one copy, no allocation per literal). It's the modern default for new files. To mutate, build a new string (`s + '!'` returns a new one) or call `.dup` to get a mutable copy. The magic comment must be the first line (or after shebang/encoding). Per-file: each file needs its own. Strings from IO, +, gsub, etc. are NOT frozen by it (only literals). Use it in new code; in gems for thread-safety.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to mutate a frozen literal (<< or gsub! raises FrozenError), or expecting it to affect non-literal strings.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: # frozen_string_literal: true (magic comment, top of file) makes string literals immutable. Prevents bugs; improves perf. Use .dup to mutate.
